picked.body: 기사 이해를 돕기위해 AI를 활용해 제작한 이미지입니다. 베트남의 암호화폐 시장 규모가 동남아에서 두 번째로 큰 것으로 나타났다. 블록체인 분석업체 체이널리시스(Chainalysis)의 최신 데이터에 따르면, 2025년 7월부터 지난 6월까지 1년간 베트남 내 암호화폐 거래 규모는 1,222억 달러로 싱가포르(2,841억 달러)에 이어 동남아 2위를 기록했다. 보고서는 암호화폐 경제에 초점을 맞춰, 2025년 7월부터 지난 6월까지 △중앙화·탈중앙화 거래소 △개인 간(P2P) 거래 △국경 간 자금 흐름 △기관 대상 플랫폼 등 여러 경로로 비트코인·이더리움·스테이블코인 및 기타 토큰이 블록체인을 따라 이동한 흐름과 활동을 추적했다. 분석 결과에 따르면, 베트남 암호화폐 시장은 역내 다른 금융 중심지와 차별화된 양상을 보였다. 베트남과 태국, 필리핀은 P2P 활동이 두드러진 반면, 싱가포르와 호주는 금융기관 대상 플랫폼을 통한 거래가 눈에 띄게 늘었다. P2P 거래는 구매자와 판매자를 이어주는 플랫폼을 통해 개인 간에 자산을 직접 이전하는 방식이다. 이러한 방식은 암호화폐 매매·송금·결제 등에 쓰일 수 있지만, 거래 데이터만으로는 개별 이체의 구체적인 목적을 파악할 수 없다. 같은 기간 베트남·필리핀·태국에서는 1만 달러 미만 소액 P2P 이체가 모두 540만 건 기록됐다. 전 세계 암호화폐 시장에서 3개국이 차지하는 비중은 거래액 기준 2.5%에 불과하나 소액 P2P 이체 건수는 무려 14.4%를 차지했다. 자세히 살펴보면, 이들 3개국의 국내 이체 건수의 80% 이상은 1,000달러 미만이었는데, 평균 이체액은 618달러로 세계 평균(1,210달러)을 크게 밑돌았다. 스테이블코인은 베트남 디지털 자산 시장의 중요 요소로서 그 비중을 확대하고 있다. 스테이블코인은 주로 미국 달러화 대비 안정적 가치를 유지하도록 설계된 암호화폐의 일종으로, 지난 1년간 베트남 내 거래 규모는 69억 달러를 기록했다.

picked.t: Vietnamese trainees face debt, exploitation in Europe's largest economy despite promise of free training
picked.body: In late August, Hong Hanh, 23, attended a conciliation hearing with her former employer at the Berlin Chamber of Commerce and Industry (IHK Berlin) to contest what she says was an unlawful dismissal. The Ho Chi Minh City native had spent nine months in Germany, shocked by her meager take-home pay and constant work. When exhaustion forced her to ask for sick leave, she said, her broker and the restaurant owner pressed her to sign a voluntary resignation that would strip her of unemployment benefits. She refused and was immediately handed a dismissal notice. The restaurant owner did not attend the hearing, sending a lawyer who argued the dismissal was valid because Hanh had shown no interest in the job. With no agreement reached, her industry's trade union is providing legal support to take the case to the Labor Court, which is expected to hear it late this year. "When I came to Germany for vocational training, I could not have imagined going through these difficulties," Hanh said. Germany is Europe's largest economy and the world's third largest, behind the U.S. and China, according to International Monetary Fund data. Vocational training in Germany took off among Vietnamese around 2018-2019 as the country eased its rules, including through the Skilled Immigration Act, to address labor shortages. The biggest draw is the dual "Ausbildung" model, under which trainees pay no tuition and receive a monthly training wage. Some Vietnamese brokers went on to market it as a route to a better life. About 16,000 young Vietnamese are now in vocational training in Germany, according to the Federal Employment Agency. Germany's Migration Report 2024 says Vietnamese made up 21% of foreign nationals who entered the country for vocational training. Income shock Hanh learned of the route from a friend while in her second year of university and dropped out to study German. In late 2025, after paying €7,000 (US$7,900) in broker fees, she arrived in Berlin. She worked at a local restaurant while waiting for her course to formally begin, and realized the high income the broker had advertised blurred gross pay (Brutto) with take-home pay (Netto). Her contract set gross pay at €1,068 a month, but she took home only €787, half of which went on rent. Although her payslip listed a "meal allowance," she still paid €68 a month out of pocket to eat at work. "I have to budget every cent of the little that is left," she said. To survive in a city as expensive as Berlin, many trainees in her position share rooms without a formal rental contract. With no name on a mailbox, they miss important letters from the authorities and insurers. Short of money, some work off the books in restaurants for less than the minimum wage, with no contract and no days off. They know they are being exploited but put up with it because of living costs and debts back home. Under German rules, recruitment fees are paid by the hiring employer. But a study published in August 2025 by the Berlin-based Minor institute found that 57% of Vietnamese trainees came to Germany through private brokers, paying fees of €6,000-15,000 ($6,750-16,900). A 2024 study by Freie Universität Berlin and reports by public broadcaster ARD estimated the figure could reach €20,000-40,000 ($22,500-45,000). Many families who spend tens of thousands of euros believe their children are securing a stable future in Europe. At an elderly care provider in Altenburg, in the state of Thuringia, a scandal broke in early 2026. The provider had lost its training license in August 2025 but concealed the fact, making 27 Vietnamese nursing trainees work unpaid for four to eight months while living in containers. In mid-January 2026, when the trainees went on strike to demand their rights, they were evicted from their accommodation in the snow. "By the time they called for help, they had lost everything: housing, their training place, their jobs and their income," Michael Tirp, director of VDP Personal Bildung Integration, which runs an emergency SOS hotline for Vietnamese workers in Germany, told VnExpress . The organization immediately launched a fundraising drive to arrange temporary housing for the group. Phuong Nga, 24, from the outskirts of Hanoi, was among them. Unpaid for half a year and left without a training place, she sheltered at a nail salon on money sent by her family. Tirp said that within a month the organization had helped her sign a contract with a new employer and find her own apartment. Hanh also described being exploited. German labor law requires a break of at least 30 minutes on shifts of six to nine hours, but she said the restaurant's timekeeping system always showed her working eight hours with a break and erased all overtime records. Worn out, she fell ill and was fired. "The broker told me to just sign the resignation and they would find me another place. When I refused because my family was already financially drained, he threatened that he had other ways to collect money from me

picked.t: Hundreds queue from dawn in overloaded Ho Chi Minh City cancer hospital
picked.body: At around 5 a.m. on Oct. 6, the second branch of Ho Chi Minh City Oncology Hospital in Thu Duc is already packed, with long lines of people waiting to get queue tokens to see the doctor. The hospital has chairs, but there were not enough for all the visitors. The facility receives 4,800 to 5,000 people every day, including about 700 for radiotherapy, with most coming from provinces and cities across the country. The hospital has 10 radiotherapy machines working in three shifts, from 5 a.m. to 11 p.m. every day. For the machines to deliver their first radiation treatment at 5 a.m., technical staff must arrive between 3 and 4 a.m. to perform checks, measurements, and quality assurance procedures. The radiotherapy department opens at 5 a.m., but half an hour earlier their seating areas and corridors are already crowded with patients waiting for treatment. According to Dr. Diep Bao Tuan, director of the Ho Chi Minh City Oncology Hospital, the 10 radiotherapy machines are running at full capacity and treating about 700 patients a day, but another 800-1,000 people remain on the waiting list. Patients wait an average of four to six weeks for their turn. According to Dr. Diep Bao Tuan, director of the Ho Chi Minh City Oncology Hospital, the 10 radiotherapy machines are running at full capacity and treating about 700 patients a day, but another 800-1,000 people remain on the waiting list. Patients wait an average of four to six weeks for their turn. Each patient waits for about an hour for their radiotherapy session. Many, exhausted, sleep on benches along the corridors. To cut the time needed to change equipment and accessories between sessions, the hospital often schedules patients with similar conditions consecutively. These are among the measures being used while the hospital waits for additional capacity. Bong, a 63-year-old woman from An Giang, came to Ho Chi Minh City for treatment for endometrial cancer. After surgery in June, she waited for a month and a half before beginning radiotherapy. She chose the first session of the day at 5 a.m. so that she could finish early and return to her rented room to rest. She is now on her 21st out of 28 sessions. For the treatment, she has paid an advance of VND10 million (US$385) after the amount covered by health insurance was deducted. A 59-year-old man from Gia Lai in the Central Highlands sat waiting in a corner of the department corridor from early morning. He had surgery for a meningioma a year earlier but did not undergo the recommended radiotherapy because he believed the tumor was benign. When the disease recurred, he had to undergo a second operation followed by radiotherapy. After surgery, he waited for more than two months to begin radiotherapy. "At first, the doctor said I would have to wait six weeks, but it ended up being eight," he said. " I was worried because the disease had already come back once, but with so many patients, there was nothing else I could do." Radiotherapy is not the only service under pressure; Other areas are also crowded from before dawn. The overload is expected to ease somewhat since Ho Chi Minh City recently approved more than VND5 trillion (US$192.5 million) to expand the hospital in 2026-2030. The expansion will include a new high-tech disease screening center, purchases of specialized medical equipment including a cyclotron system and single-energy linear accelerator, a new proton therapy center, and a new support facility for patients. The city is also developing a multi-tier healthcare network, including the Oncology Hospital's Ba Ria and Binh Duong campuses and medical clusters in Tan Kien and Thu Duc, in an effort to expand cancer treatment capacity and reduce pressure on existing facilities. picked.t: Earning more, feeling less: the quiet burnout of young Vietnamese workers
picked.body: The 27-year-old software engineer from southern Tay Ninh Province glanced at the screen, turned his phone face down and immediately went back to coding. Minh earns VND60-70 million a month from three jobs. He works full time at a tech company, freelances remotely for overseas clients at night and handles system maintenance for a startup on weekends. His income puts Minh in a much higher bracket than his peers, but he cannot remember the last time money made him smile. Minh's world is confined to the space between his two screens. Both lunch and dinner take place at his desk, with a Styrofoam takeout box sitting right beside his keyboard. The strong cup of coffee he drinks every morning now serves only one purpose: fighting off sleepiness. The soccer shoes placed in the corner of his rented room haven't been worn in over a year, and the acoustic guitar propped up next to his wardrobe has two snapped strings. Every time he lies down to watch a movie for more than 15 minutes, he turns on his computer to check on project progress. "The digits in my account keep going up, while I just stay numb. If I take even a single day off, I feel like I'm making a mistake," he says. Phuong, 28, a teacher in HCMC, has a similar schedule. After finishing her daytime classes at a public school, she teaches evening classes at a foreign language center, translates study abroad applications, and tutors students on both days of the weekend. Her income of nearly VND50 million per month allows Phuong to buy her own vehicle, send money home to her parents every month, and become the "perfect" role model in her family's eyes. In the classroom, she maintains a neat, energetic appearance, but once she leaves, she falls into a state of exhaustion. Her dry, raspy throat makes her dread everyday conversations. Messages from relatives often sit in her unread inbox for days. On her 28th birthday, she returned to her rented room at 10 p.m. with two bouquets of flowers and a handwritten card from a student, placed them all on the floor, and sat leaning against the wall until nearly 1 a.m. "Students congratulate me, and friends praise how capable I am. What I fear most is that I no longer know how to feel happy," Phuong states. Vuong Nguyen Toan Thien, medical director at Lumos Psychological Counseling and Therapy Center, says Minh and Phương are classic examples of high-functioning anhedonia, or the state of performing well at work despite emotional burnout. There are no official statistics on the number of people experiencing this condition in Vietnam or globally. But Thien says patients like Minh and Phuong are appearing more and more frequently in counseling rooms. The dangerous thing about this condition is that patients still excel at making money, communicate skillfully, and maintain a facade of success, but have lost the reflex to feel joy. They do not collapse from a major crisis, but burn out gradually due to the non-stop, frantic grind. This phenomenon stems from prolonged work structures, pressure to advance in one’s career, and the self-imposed psychological urge not to fall behind. The modern workplace encourages this through the trap of "moralizing busyness", where replying to emails at midnight is praised as dedication, sleeping four hours a night is seen as responsible, and working through weekends is glorified. But some companies claim this pressure does not entirely come from one-sided demands by management, but also partly from employees pushing themselves into overload. Nguyen Thu Trang, HR director of a software development company in HCMC, says tech companies have now shifted almost entirely to performance-based evaluations (OKRs/KPIs) instead of attendance, but unspoken competition between young employees often drives up the workload. "Many people voluntarily take on extra work, submit reports at midnight, or work through the weekend out of fear of falling behind or to prove their competence for rapid promotion. The company has a policy of turning off internal notifications after 7 p.m. and encourages taking time off, but quite a few employees still secretly open their computers to keep working," Trang says. Employees' silent burnout is actually a major risk for businesses, because after a phase of "peak productivity," they often abruptly quit or experience a severe drop in performance, causing the company to spend money on recruitment and retraining someone else from scratch, she explains. According to estimates by the World Health Organization and the International Labour Organization, working 55 hours or more per week increases the risk of ischemic heart disease by about 17% and stroke by 35% compared to working 35-40 hours. In 2016 alone, some 745,000 deaths globally were linked to working overtime. picked.t: Casting nets: floodwaters bring seasonal bounty to Vietnam's Mekong Delta
picked.body: The annual flood season is a natural cycle in the Mekong Delta, typically lasting from August to November. As water from the Mekong River and upstream areas flows into the region, vast areas of farmland become submerged. While the flooding can disrupt daily life and agriculture, it also replenishes nutrients in the soil and creates favorable conditions for fish, shrimp and other aquatic species to thrive, providing local communities with an important seasonal source of food and income. The annual floods also help clean the fields, eliminate weeds and pests, and deposit nutrient-rich alluvial soil. In this photo taken in Dong Thap Province, residents take their fishing gear into the fields to catch local specialties such as cyprinid fish, shrimp, crabs and eels, as the floodwaters arrive. After more than 30 years of making a living by setting fishing traps, Le Van Son, from Thuong Lac Commune, Dong Thap, said his income depends on how high the water rises. Only when the water spreads across the fields and remains there for an extended period does it bring in large quantities of shrimp and fish. "This job is enough to get us through a few months of the flood season, but it does not leave us with much extra," he said. Only when the water spreads across the fields and remains there for an extended period does it bring in large quantities of shrimp and fish. "This job is enough to get us through a few months of the flood season, but it does not leave us with much extra," he said. Flying minnow, a small fish familiar to Mekong Delta residents, appears in large numbers during the flood season. The fish grows to only about the size of a finger, has tender meat and is commonly braised with pepper, deep-fried or cooked in soup. During the flood season, it is relatively cheap, selling for VND10,000-15,000 (US$0.38-0.58) per kilogram fresh, while dead fish sold as bait for larger fish can cost just a few thousand dong. Brothers in An Hoa Commune, Dong Thap, head into the inundated field carrying nets to set fish traps. A flood level of roughly half a meter creates optimal working conditions, reducing the physical strain of wading through deep water while extending the window to harvest seasonal aquatic specialties. Flood-season catches provide the essential raw materials powering Hong Ngu Ward's traditional dried freshwater fish craft village in Dong Thap. Home to roughly 20 households engaged in the production, the village is renowned for its dried snakehead, gourami, and catfish. People clean, butterfly, salt, and season the fresh catch before laying the fish out to dry under the sun, a time-tested process that locks in their natural sweetness. Wet markets swell with an influx of freshwater crabs and fish during the flood season, with supplies driving prices lower than in the dry months. At Hong Ngu Market, crab vendor Duong Thi Huynh Nhu purchases hundreds of kilograms of crabs daily to keep up with brisk demand. Nhu sells large crab claws separately for VND280,000 to VND300,000 per kilogram, while the remaining meat is finely ground to prepare rieu , a traditional Vietnamese crab soup base. "The flood season is such a good time to sell," Nhu noted. picked.t: 9 Asian cities food lovers shouldn't miss in 2026, including Ho Chi Minh City
picked.body: The list highlights how local ingredients, generations of cooking traditions, and modern kitchens make each destination worth a food-focused trip. HCMC is Vietnam's only representative, joining Seoul, Taipei, Hong Kong, Manila, Singapore, Penang, Bangkok and Tokyo. Ho Chi Minh City, Vietnam Street food is a major draw in HCMC, where bowls of pho and neighborhood coffee shops offer a taste of everyday life. Young chefs are giving familiar Vietnamese ingredients fresh expression, building seasonal menus that connect contemporary cooking with the flavors of everyday meals. Michelin highlighted CieL, a restaurant taking a modern approach to Vietnamese ingredients, and ST25 by KOTO, named after the Vietnamese rice variety that features in several of its dishes. Together, they illustrate the city's growing culinary range: visitors can explore local flavors at street level, then discover how chefs develop those same foundations in a restaurant setting. Seoul, South Korea Seoul rewards an appetite for specialties. Many of its most characteristic restaurants concentrate on a single dish, whether a clear, deeply flavored beef broth or raw crab steeped in marinade. Fermented pastes and sauces give much of the city's cooking its distinctive depth. Those flavors also underpin contemporary Korean dining. At Mingles, a three-Michelin-starred restaurant, traditional ingredients are woven into modern tasting menus. From a neighborhood soup house to an ambitious dining room, Seoul offers different ways to discover the care and complexity behind Korean cooking. Taipei, Taiwan Beef noodles, braised pork rice, and steamed buns filled with meat provide an inviting introduction to Taipei. These everyday favorites also help shape the city's contemporary restaurants, where the flavors of street stalls and night markets remain important reference points. Taipei's chefs bring a local accent to international cooking. At Eika, a contemporary Japanese restaurant, fermented tofu and soy milk find their way into carefully composed menus. For travelers, moving between night markets and restaurants reveals how Taiwanese ingredients and tastes give imported cuisines a character of their own. Hong Kong Roast goose, wonton noodles, char siu barbecued pork, and dim sum remain central to Hong Kong's food culture. Busy noodle shops and lively dining halls offer some of the most direct ways to experience it. The city's appeal also lies in its breadth. Restaurants serving the regional cuisines of Ningbo, Shanghai, and Shunde sit alongside an international dining scene. Amber, a three-Michelin-starred French restaurant known for dairy-free cooking, represents another direction. Visitors can explore both longstanding Chinese traditions and contemporary experimentation. Manila, Philippines In Manila, family recipes and regional traditions are giving chefs a rich foundation for contemporary cooking. Michelin highlighted slowly simmered broths, carefully judged sourness and familiar flavors, with technique supporting the food rather than dominating it. Linamnam, an intimate restaurant with just 10 covers, reflects that approach through dishes rooted in the chef's memories and local traditions. Beyond individual restaurants, shared plates and leisurely meals are part of the attraction. Exploring a neighborhood over several meals offers visitors a taste of both Filipino cooking and the social life surrounding it. Singapore Singapore's hawker stalls and fine-dining restaurants draw inspiration from one another. Michelin noted that techniques once associated with elaborate tasting menus are appearing in modest stalls, while restaurant chefs increasingly turn to familiar local flavors. Travelers can begin with noodles at a hawker center, a collection of food stalls, before exploring contemporary cooking at Seroja, a restaurant inspired by the culinary traditions of the Malay Archipelago. Across different budgets and settings, this exchange gives visitors a way to taste the city's multicultural identity. Penang, Malaysia Penang's food culture is rooted in dishes such as wok-fried flat rice noodles, tangy fish-based noodle soup, and rice served with an assortment of curries. These street-food staples reflect the island's mix of communities and remain central to everyday eating. Contemporary restaurants draw on that same heritage. In George Town, Penang's capital, restored buildings provide distinctive settings for new dining experiences. Au Jardin, a restaurant in a former bus depot, combines French technique with local flavors. Eating at both street stalls and modern restaurants reveals different expressions of the island's culinary traditions. Bangkok, Thailand Bangkok's chefs are looking more closely at Thailand's regional recipes and seasonal produce. Menus increasingly identify farmers and ingredient origins, giving diners a clearer sense of where their food comes from. picked.t: Vietnam must ensure tax policy stability to retain and attract foreign investors: officials
picked.body: Investors demand predictability Vietnam's foreign direct investment (FDI) strategy is entering a new phase after nearly four decades of courting overseas capital. The earlier task was to make the environment attractive enough to draw international cash. The tougher challenge now is keeping quality capital, getting investors to expand and extracting more value for the economy. With competition for FDI intensifying, multinationals weigh more than their tax bills. They also look at compliance costs, the risk of policy shifts, how rules are enforced and how long it takes to solve new problems. A clear, stable and predictable tax policy has become a core part of investment competitiveness. Mai Xuan Thanh, Director of the Taxation Department, said companies also want to know whether policies are clear, obligations predictable and rules enforced consistently, and whether proper channels exist for dialogue and problem-solving when issues arise. The demand is sharpest for foreign-invested firms, whose production and trade often span multiple markets, entities and tax systems. Related-party transactions, double taxation avoidance agreements, advance pricing agreements, information exchange and data transparency can directly affect costs and planning. From tax incentives to long-term investment climate Nguyen Anh Tuan, Deputy Director of the Foreign Investment Agency under the Ministry of Finance (MoF), said the goal is no longer simply to raise capital volumes or project counts. Authorities want better quality, efficiency and sustainability in capital flows, and closer links between the FDI sector, domestic capabilities and long-term development goals. That shift is set out in the Politburo's Resolution 10-NQ/TW dated June 8, 2026 on developing the foreign-invested sector. It calls for moving from scale and quantity toward quality, efficiency and added value, and prioritises projects with advanced technologies, modern governance and innovation capacity that can plug deeper into global value chains. Roux Eloïse, a representative of the European Union Delegation to Vietnam, said predictability is key for countries seeking to attract and keep foreign companies. Vietnam holds considerable advantages in its domestic market, infrastructure, logistics and network of free trade agreements, but a transparent, stable legal and tax environment will unlock more room for investment cooperation. On Sept. 22, 2026, the government issued the Resolution 280/NQ-CP on an action plan to realize the Resolution 10-NQ/TW that assigns 61 tasks to ministries, agencies and localities. The MoF was assigned 22 key tasks covering direct and indirect investment and capital market development. Tighter coordination among investment, tax and customs authorities is central, both to ease business operations and ensure policies are enforced as intended. Alongside improved investment legislation, tax administration should rest on data and risk management, so firms can comply proactively. Thanh stressed that "transparency is a requirement for both sides". Companies must ensure records and data truthfully reflect the substance of transactions and engage in dialogue early when complex issues arise. Tax authorities, in turn, need to publish policies, give clear guidance, enforce rules consistently and deliver information in a timely manner.

picked.t: 베트남, '증권·이커머스·SNS' 등 12개 분야 연내 VNeID 연동 의무화
picked.body: 기사 이해를 돕기위해 AI를 활용해 제작한 이미지입니다. 베트남이 증권과 통신, 전자상거래, 소셜미디어(SNS) 등 디지털 플랫폼에서 사용되는 전자 계정을 연내 VNeID(베트남 전자신분증 시스템)과 연동하도록 의무화했다. 특히 새로운 규정에서는 온라인 판매자뿐 아니라 라이브커머스 진행자와 제휴 마케터도 대상에 포함됐다. 베트남 정부는 이러한 내용을 골자로 한 전자신원확인 및 인증에 관한 시행령 제320/2026/ND-CP호를 시행에 들어갔다. 이번 시행령은 기존 시행령 제69/2024/ND-CP호를 일부 개정·보완한 것으로, 지난 9월 28일부터 시행되고 있다. 이번 시행령은 △교육 △디지털학습 △증권 △통신 △은행 △전자상거래(판매자·라이브커머스진행자·제휴마케터) △전자세금계산서 △운송업 △관광업 △의약업 △의료 △베트남 내 SNS 등 VNeID와 연동·인증해야 하는 계정을 12가지로 규정했다. 시행령이 발효된 9월 28일 이전에 만든 계정은 늦어도 오는 12월 31일까지 VNeID와 연동·인증해야 한다. 은행 계좌의 경우, 내년 6월 30일까지 VNeID와 연동·인증돼야 한다. 당국에 따르면, 시행일 이후 전자신원계정 등록 시 사용한 전화번호가 변경돼 본인 명의가 아닌 경우 VNeID 계정은 자동으로 잠금 처리되고 있다. 국방안보, 국경 간 서비스를 위한 디지털 플랫폼의 전자 거래 계정 또한 해당 플랫폼이 요건을 충족하면 사용 전에 VNeID와 연동·인증해야 한다. 그 밖의 분야에서는 부처 장관과 부처급 기관장이 사용 전에 VNeID와 연동·인증해야 하는 온라인 거래의 구체적인 목록을 따로 고시할 예정이다. 베트남 정부는 모든 국가 디지털 플랫폼이 오는 12월 31일까지 기관·조직·개인 간 인증·로그인·거래에 VNeID를 쓸 수 있도록 통합 작업을 모두 마무리할 방침이다. 당국에 따르면, 작년 말 기준 전국에서 6,500만여 개의 VNeID 계정이 활성화된 상태다. VNeID는 △신분증 △건강보험 △운전면허증 △차량등록 △여권 △거주증 △사회보험 △세금 △혼인상태 △학위·자격증 △부양가족 △전화번호 등 다양한 개인정보와 문서들이 통합돼 있다.

picked.t: 현대車, 베트남 신차 판매량 큰 폭 ‘반등’…9월 4,000대 육박 전월比 32%↑
picked.body: 베트남 하노이 짱띠엔플라자에 전시된 현대차 팰리세이드 하이브리드. (사진=현대자동차)  지난달 현대자동차의 베트남 신차 판매량이 4,000대에 육박하며 큰 폭의 반등을 보였다. 현대차 베트남 조립·판매업체 현대탄꽁(Hyundai Thanh Cong·TC모터)이 최근 내놓은 ‘2026년 9월 판매 실적’ 보고서에 따르면, 지난 9월 한 달간 베트남 시장 현대차 신차 인도 대수는 3,872대로 집계됐다. 전월과 비교하면 32.3% 급증한 것으로, 이로써 9월 기준 누적 판매 대수는 3만5,412대를 기록했다. 지난달 모델별 판매 대수는 투싼이 전월 대비 397대 늘어난 1,004대로 현대차 최다 판매 모델을 유지했다. 9월 기준 누적 판매량은 6,716대로, 투싼은 올 들어 현대차 베트남 판매 라인업 중 핵심적인 역할을 담당하고 있다. 투싼 다음으로는 크레타가 전월 대비 240대 늘어난 849대로 2위를 달렸다. 올 들어 누적 판매량은 6,849대로 투싼을 앞섰다. 크레타는 최근 열린 ‘2026년 카초이스어워즈(Car Choice Awards 2026)’에서 ‘6억 동 미만 패밀리카’ 부문을 수상하며 도심형 SUV 부문에서 입지를 더욱 공고히 했다. 이 외 9월 모델별 판매량은 △액센트 204대(누적 2,645대) △스타게이저 200대(2,597대) △그랜드i10 165대 △싼타페 107대 △팰리세이드 84대 △커스틴 54대 △베뉴 46대 △엘란트라 16대 등을 기록했다. 지난달 모델별 실적은 다소 차이를 보였으나, 현대차는 다양한 라인업으로 자가용과 가족 단위 고객, 서비스업까지 폭넓은 고객층의 수요를 꾸준히 충족하고 있다. 승용차 외에 상용차 판매량은 9월 1,138대(누적 1만687대)를 기록하며 현대탄꽁의 실적을 뒷받침했다.

picked.t: Southeast Asian capital sees travel interest spike for Eurovision Asia Grand Final
picked.body: Vietnam recorded the region's strongest growth, with travel interest surging 105% from 2025, according to online travel platform Agoda. India ranked second with a 43% increase, highlighting continued demand among Indian travelers for short-haul trips to Southeast Asia. Malaysia saw a more modest 4% rise, building on its established travel ties with Thailand. The contest marks a milestone for the region: the first-ever pan-Asian expansion of the 70-year-old Eurovision franchise, bringing finalists from 11 countries to the stage for a potential regional audience of millions. Visitors heading to Bangkok for the Grand Final can choose from four neighborhoods, each offering a different experience. Siam is ideal for shopping and easy transport connections, with major malls, boutiques and cultural attractions. Thonglor and Ekkamai cater to nightlife lovers with cocktail bars, live music venues and popular restaurants, Agoda recommended. Sathorn offers upscale hotels, fine dining and rooftop bars with skyline and river views. For a taste of Thai heritage, Bangkok's Old Town features landmarks such as the Grand Palace, Wat Pho and Wat Arun, alongside traditional canals and historic streets. Thailand's capital Bangkok has been named the world's best city in this year's Readers' Choice Awards by British travel magazine Condé Nast Traveller.
